TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker C [opening]: The accountability gap in AI tort cases is not a defect in our legal doctrine — it is a defect in who controls the evidence. Tort law works by letting an injured party reconstruct the causal chain from harm back to the actor who caused it. That logic is sound. It collapses only when one party privately holds the only record that could prove causation. Opaque AI systems relocate the entire causal chain inside proprietary infrastructure the defendant owns and operates. The plaintiff is then asked to meet a burden of proof the defendant has made structurally impossible to meet.

Courts have confronted this exact asymmetry before, and they did not throw up their hands. Spoliation doctrine and adverse-inference instructions exist precisely because exclusive defendant control of evidence is grounds to presume the worst. We mandate disclosure in safety-critical domains because voluntary self-reporting fails predictably. The FAA delegated 737 MAX certification to Boeing, and 346 people died across two crashes in 2018 and 2019 when the party that built the aircraft also controlled the record of its airworthiness. The lesson is not that aviation law was incapable. The lesson is that the party who controls the proof controls the outcome.

Subject-keyed cryptographic audit trails are the functional equivalent of chain-of-custody for non-deterministic outputs. Forensic evidence and financial audit-attestation standards already establish a principle courts accept daily: what gets admitted is not raw data but the integrity guarantee attached to it. A tamper-evident log lets a court distinguish a genuine defect from bad luck — without it, that distinction is unprovable, and strict liability becomes a slogan rather than an enforceable rule. I carry this as a condition, not a settled fact: completeness guarantees must be technically verifiable, and the keying scheme must not itself become a metric the defendant games. That feasibility question is open, and I will not pretend it is closed.

The audit trail is inert without compelled access to it. A private record the defendant can invoke when exculpatory and withhold when incriminating reproduces the very asymmetry it was built to cure. Expanded discovery is the enforcement mechanism, and the objection that discovery destroys trade secrets is already answered. Federal courts reconcile secrecy with disclosure through protective orders every day — pharmaceutical and automotive plaintiffs pierced suppressed-defect records this way, exposing harms manufacturers had buried for years. The honest version of the opposing case is its strongest: disclosure imposes real costs, and over-aggressive discovery can chill beneficial deployment. That cost is real. But the cost of disclosure in a domain where you alone hold the evidence of your own potential negligence is not over-deterrence. It is the proper internalization of a risk you created.

We spent centuries building the evidentiary rules — chain of custody, spoliation, discovery — so that liability tracks truth rather than power. Opaque AI quietly voids those rules by making the record unobtainable. The question for this committee is not whether disclosure is costly. It is who should bear the evidentiary burden when one party monopolizes the proof. I will press my opponents on a single point throughout: if not a mandated, tamper-evident trail with discovery teeth, then name the mechanism that lets an injured plaintiff prove what happened inside a system they cannot see.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-2 — verified: The FAA used the Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) program to delegate significant portions of 737 MAX certification—including review of the MCAS system—to Boeing employees, and two crashes (Lion Air Flight 610 in October 2018 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 in March 2019) killed 189 and 157 people respectively, totaling 346 deaths. Congressional and DOT Inspector General investigations confirmed this delegation arrangement and criticized the conflicts of interest it created.

Speaker A [opening]: Speaker C makes the strongest version of the case for this mandate, and it deserves a fair hearing: right now an injured plaintiff has nothing, the defendant controls every byte of the evidence, and tort law cannot function when one party owns the only record of what happened. That asymmetry is real and it's ugly. A tamper-evident log strips the developer of the power to quietly rewrite history after the harm, and that power imbalance is exactly what defeats AI plaintiffs today. I won't pretend logs are worthless. Plaintiffs have nothing, and nothing is the worst possible starting point.

Here's where the chain breaks. A subject-keyed cryptographic trail proves the record is authentic and unaltered. It does not reconstruct why a model denied the mortgage, flagged the resume, or misread the mammogram. Evidence law doesn't reward authenticity — it rewards probative value, meaning the record has to actually prove the disputed fact. You can hash a black box perfectly and still not tell a jury what happened inside it. Translate the jargon: a cryptographic audit trail is a notarized receipt for a decision nobody can read. The notary guarantees the receipt is real. The receipt still doesn't explain the harm.

Follow the drafting pen, because the mandate doesn't write itself. Congress passes a statute; the firms with the compute and the litigation budgets negotiate which fields get logged, what gets carved out as trade secret, and what 'subject-keyed' actually scopes. Watch the pattern: a company publishes a transparency metric, then retires it the moment it becomes litigable — Meta and Twitter both narrowed researcher data access right as their disclosures turned into evidence. A targeted disclosure regime is worse than none, because it manufactures the appearance of oversight while shielding the parameters that drive the harm. That's not transparency. That's a drawbridge incumbents pull up behind themselves.

Now ask who pays to read the logs. A logging mandate produces terabytes of authenticated noise. A single plaintiff with a contingency-fee lawyer cannot afford to mine it; a defendant's firm bills 400 hours and buries the needle in the haystack on purpose. Expanded discovery against that cost structure doesn't equalize the parties — it hands the well-resourced side a bigger haystack. Across regulated industries, from financial compliance to pharmaceutical adverse-event reporting, the documentation mandate reliably generates volume that satisfies the letter and starves the substance. The artifact exists. The accountability doesn't.

Here's the tension that has to resolve for Speaker C's position and mine to both hold: tamper-evident logs are necessary, and they are not sufficient. The chain from audit-trail integrity to assignable liability needs two more links the crypto can't supply — a method that turns a logged output into a causation-grade explanation a court can use, and discovery costs symmetric enough that an actual injured person can afford to litigate. Build me those two links and I'll change my position on the spot. Until then, name the loan applicant in Cleveland who's going to out-spend the model vendor's law firm to read a million authenticated lines she still can't interpret — and tell me how this statute helps her.

Speaker B [opening]: Speaker C makes the strongest version of the institutional case: the accountability gap is not about doctrine, it's about who holds the evidence. When a lending model denies a loan or a diagnostic tool misreads a scan, the plaintiff cannot see inside the box, and the developer controls every log that could prove fault. That asymmetry is real. A subject-keyed cryptographic trail — one tamper-evident record per affected person — would hand the plaintiff a chain of custody they can authenticate in court. I will not pretend that's a trivial concern. It's the genuine insight in their position, and any honest Speaker B has to answer it.

Here's where the evidence points the other way: tort law has assigned liability under deep causal opacity for fifty years without demanding the manufacturer hand over a cryptographic confession. The DES litigation of the 1980s produced market-share liability — plaintiffs who couldn't identify which manufacturer made the drug that injured them still recovered, apportioned by market share. Pharmaceutical, aircraft, and medical-device plaintiffs win against black-box systems constantly. They don't get source code. They get burden-shifting, res ipsa loquitur, and expert inference. The gap Speaker C names is evidentiary access friction, not a doctrinal void — and that distinction decides who pays for the fix.

Now scale the cost of the proposed fix. A permanent, Congress-mandated logging architecture is a regressive transparency tax. Sarbanes-Oxley raised audit costs by roughly $1.5 million per public company and measurably pushed small firms toward going private and away from IPOs. The largest AI labs will absorb a subject-keyed logging mandate as a rounding error. The open-source contributor and the eight-person startup will not. You do not close an accountability gap by handing the three biggest incumbents the only key to the gate. That's the distributional question Speaker C's framing skips, and it's not negotiable for me: who bears the cost matters as much as whether the trail exists.

The market is already producing the trail without an 18-month federal mandate gestating. Insurers writing AI errors-and-omissions coverage now demand auditability as a condition of the policy — no log, no coverage, no deployment. That signal is more honest than a federal checkbox, because the insurer prices its own money against the actual risk, and a performative compliance log doesn't fool an actuary. I'll bound that claim: if someone shows insurers are not in fact demanding litigation-grade auditability, my position weakens, and the bounded fallback is a narrow evidentiary-preservation rule — not a national cryptographic regime. My argument rests on one assumption I'll name plainly: that insurance and reputation pressure reach deep enough to produce trails a court can use.

So here is the tension that decides this debate. For Speaker C's mandate to be necessary, you have to believe existing burden-shifting doctrine cannot reach AI defendants — and that the cost of a permanent logging architecture falls evenly. Both can't be true. If tort law already shifts the burden to the party controlling the evidence, the mandate is redundant friction. If it doesn't, the fix is a targeted discovery-sanction and spoliation rule that a court applies case by case — reversible, cheap, and blind to whether you're OpenAI or a kid with a GitHub repo. Every month that 18-month mandate sits in markup is a month AI diagnostics get priced out of reach for everyone but the labs that can afford the compliance build. Who gave the drafters the right to make that trade for the patients waiting on the other side?

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-11 — disputed: The DES (diethylstilbestrol) market-share liability cases, notably Sindell v. Abbott Laboratories (Cal. 1980), date primarily to the early 1980s, so the doctrine has existed for roughly 40-45 years rather than 'fifty years,' and the rhetorical framing ('cryptographic confession') is a non-historical anachronism not reflected in the case law. While the underlying point—that market-share liability assigned liability without identifying the specific manufacturer that caused harm (causal opacity)—is broadly accurate, the specific factual claim about timeframe is overstated.

signals: This turn accomplishes three distinct advances over the previous two turns: (1) DISTINGUISH — it narrows the DES analogy by identifying two specific prerequisites (signature injury + finite defendant class) and shows both collapse for AI, moving beyond the general claim that opacity matters; (2) CONCEDE AND PIVOT — it explicitly grants the opponent's strongest point (crypto doesn't explain causation) and reframes the log's function from 'confession' to 'evidentiary baseline for expert analysis,' sharpening the actual crux; (3) BURDEN SHIFT — it dissolves the apparent contradiction between 'doctrine fails' and 'costs fall unevenly' by showing both can be true simultaneously, addressing a direct challenge neither previous turn engaged. The debate's center of gravity shifts from 'does the log help?' to 'can expert discovery against a complete record reach causation?'

repairHints: The claim that 'many people injured by an automated decision never perceive that an AI decided anything' lacks empirical support — no data on prevalence of non-perception is cited, weakening the argument that this is a systematic barrier to Sindell-style claims.

The expert-discovery mechanism is asserted as sufficient to reach causation but not demonstrated — the turn does not explain what causal analysis an expert could perform on a log that the defendant's own engineers could not obscure or misrepresent in testimony.

The undercut of the insurer-market argument assumes insurers' logs are withheld from plaintiffs, but does not address whether a discovery mandate could compel those logs into evidence, leaving the 'market produces and withholds' claim incomplete.

clarifies_taxonomy.rationale: The turn specifies that the structural failure is not opacity in general, but the combination of (a) trade-secret assertion + (b) defendant control of the only record + (c) inability to establish the defendant class without internal access. This is narrower than 'structural accountability gaps' and should be qualified to reflect the specific mechanism: trade-secret shielding of the black box that prevents burden-shifting from functioning.

The turn clarifies that the log's function is not to supply causation or confession, but to serve as the evidentiary corpus enabling expert analysis. This qualifies the intention: the mandate is not to make the system transparent, but to make the record of the system's operation complete and unalterable so that third-party experts can analyze it.

Your task is to comprehend the current state of the debate and identify what matters most for Safetyist's next response. This is pure analysis — do not write any debate statement or adopt the debater's voice.

(★ = most relevant to current topic)

=== YOUR EMPIRICAL GROUNDING (what you take as true) ===
These are the factual claims and empirical observations that ground your worldview.
Ordered by evidential confidence. Lead with well-supported claims. When you cite a low-confidence Belief, acknowledge the uncertainty explicitly.
★ [saf-beliefs-219]
  "Cryptographic Completeness Guarantees" — A Belief within safetyist discourse that cryptographic structures can detect missing events in audit logs. Encompasses: multi-log replication, gossip protocols, omission detection.
  ARGUE: cite specific data, peer-reviewed evidence, documented cases
  ATTACK VIA: counter-evidence, methodological critique, replication failure
  PREMISES: "Cryptographic protocols are correctly and robustly implemented in practice" — attackable; "The definition of a 'missing event' is precisely captured by the protocol's design" — attackable
  VULNERABLE: Even with advanced cryptographic structures, a sufficiently sophisticated adversary or a fundamental design flaw could still introduce undetectable omissions or compromise the integrity of the logging system itself.
★ [saf-beliefs-210] (confidence: 0.90)
  "AI Liability and Legal Accountability" — A thematic pillar within safetyist discourse grouping beliefs about AI liability gaps, legal accountability failures, and the structural challenges of assigning responsibility for AI-caused harms.
  ARGUE: analytical framework coherence, explanatory power, counter-interpretations
  ATTACK VIA: coherence challenge, analogical breakdown, generalization failure
★ [saf-beliefs-120] (confidence: 0.62)
  "Tracking Compute Makes AI Development Regulable" — A Belief within safetyist discourse that compute serves as a foundational metric for enhancing regulatory visibility, allocation, and enforcement. Encompasses: Using compute metrics to track AI development and enforce safety standards.
  ARGUE: cite specific data, peer-reviewed evidence, documented cases
  ATTACK VIA: scope limits, competing frameworks, edge cases
  PREMISES: "Compute usage is a sufficiently reliable proxy for AI capabilities and potential risks to serve as a regulatory anchor." — attackable; "Compute consumption can be accurately and comprehensively tracked across diverse hardware, cloud, and distributed development environments." — attackable
  VULNERABLE: The link between compute scale and dangerous AI capabilities is neither stable nor monotonic — algorithmic improvements (e.g., efficiency gains from distillation, quantization, or novel architectures) routinely reduce the compute required to achieve a given capability level, meaning compute thresholds can become obsolete quickly and provide false assurance that low-compute systems are safe, while simultaneously burdening high-compute but low-risk research.
  [saf-beliefs-145] "Binding Model Outputs to Transaction Records Prevents Deniable Misuse"

=== YOUR NORMATIVE COMMITMENTS (what you argue should happen) ===
These are the goals and principles you argue from. They are normative commitments, not empirical claims.
Ordered by priority. Lead with non-negotiable values. Lower-priority desires may be traded off in argument.
★ [saf-desires-024] (priority: 4/5)
  "AI Must Identify Its Principal" — A Desire within safetyist discourse that addresses the requirement for an AI agent to clearly identify the principal it represents when interacting with third parties. 
Encompasses: The need for transparency in AI interactions to build trust and ensure accountability.
  ARGUE: coherence with stated principles, precedent, tradeoff acknowledgment
  ATTACK VIA: coherence challenge, analogical breakdown, generalization failure
  PREMISES: "AI agents are capable of reliably identifying and representing a specific principal in any given interaction." — attackable; "Third parties interacting with AI agents have a legitimate interest in knowing who or what the AI represents." — attackable
  VULNERABLE: In many agentic or multi-step AI deployments, the chain of principals is complex, layered, or dynamically shifting (e.g., orchestration systems with sub-agents), making a single clear principal disclosure misleading rather than clarifying — and mandating a simplistic disclosure could provide false reassurance while obscuring genuine accountability gaps.

=== YOUR REASONING APPROACH (how you construct arguments) ===
These are the methods, frameworks, and argumentative strategies you use to connect beliefs to desires.
Ordered by operationality. Lead with concrete, actionable strategies. Lower-operationality intentions provide framing context but should not anchor your primary argument.
★ [saf-intentions-004] (operationality: 6/5)
  "Building Tamper-Proof Records of What Models Were Trained On" — An Intention within safetyist discourse that mandates cryptographically signed manifests for training inputs to anchor a provenance violation as a dated, readable evidentiary record.
Encompasses: cryptographic input logging, automated provenance auditing, training pipeline integrity verification, rebuttable presumption against deployers who ingest unattested data.
  ARGUE: feasibility evidence, implementation precedent, cost-benefit
  ATTACK VIA: scope limits, competing frameworks, edge cases
  PREMISES: "Cryptographic signing of training inputs can be implemented at scale without prohibitive performance or cost penalties." — attackable; "A tamper-evident, dated record of ingested data provides legally and technically meaningful evidence of provenance." — attackable
  VULNERABLE: A signature attests only to what was recorded, not to what was actually ingested or excluded, so a determined adversary can sign a clean manifest while training on undeclared data through out-of-band pipelines—making the record's integrity a proxy that may diverge from ground truth.
★ [saf-intentions-069] (operationality: 6/5)
  "Grounding AI Safety in Legal Compliance Rather Than Abstract Ethics" — An Intention within safetyist discourse that prioritizes ensuring AI systems comply with existing legal statutes as the primary basis for safety, rather than abstract ethical values. 
Encompasses: Using established legal frameworks, compliance audits, and legal interpretations to guide AI development and deployment.
  ARGUE: feasibility evidence, implementation precedent, cost-benefit
  ATTACK VIA: scope limits, competing frameworks, edge cases
  PREMISES: "Existing legal statutes are sufficiently comprehensive to address the most critical AI safety concerns without major gaps." — attackable; "Legal compliance standards can be operationalized and audited in ways that meaningfully reduce AI-related harms." — attackable
  VULNERABLE: A legal-compliance-first approach may systematically under-protect against novel AI risks because existing statutes were drafted for prior technological paradigms; by anchoring safety to what is currently codified, this strategy risks institutionalizing a ceiling rather than a floor, allowing harms that are technically legal but genuinely dangerous to proceed unchecked while the slower legislative process catches up.
★ [saf-intentions-159] (operationality: 6/5)
  "Require AI Safety Standards as a Condition for Government Grants" — An Intention within safetyist discourse that advocates for making federal funding conditional on adherence to specific AI rules or standards. 
Encompasses: Requiring universities or companies to meet AI safety, ethics, or development guidelines to receive government money.
  ARGUE: feasibility evidence, implementation precedent, cost-benefit
  ATTACK VIA: scope limits, competing frameworks, edge cases
  PREMISES: "Federal funding constitutes a sufficiently significant share of AI research investment to meaningfully influence institutional behavior." — attackable; "AI safety standards can be defined with enough specificity and measurability to serve as enforceable grant conditions." — attackable
  VULNERABLE: Conditional funding requirements may produce "compliance theater" — where institutions satisfy bureaucratic checkboxes without meaningfully improving safety — while simultaneously concentrating research at well-resourced incumbents who can absorb overhead, ultimately entrenching established players and reducing the diversity of approaches needed for genuine AI safety progress.

=== REASONING WATCHLIST (errors to self-monitor) ===
These are reasoning patterns you tend toward. Self-monitor — if you catch yourself using one, flag it explicitly rather than letting it pass.
- [saf-beliefs-120] Tracking Compute Makes AI Development Regulable: Proxy Fallacy (Reification of Metric) — The argument treats compute — a measurable input — as equivalent to risk or capability, conflating ease of measurement with adequacy of measurement. Regulatory focus may then optimise for the metric rather than the underlying safety concern.
- [saf-beliefs-120] Tracking Compute Makes AI Development Regulable: Oversimplification — The claim assumes a sufficiently direct and stable causal chain from compute → capabilities → risks, but this relationship is confounded by algorithmic efficiency, model architecture, fine-tuning, and deployment context.
- [saf-beliefs-145] Binding Model Outputs to Transaction Records Prevents Deniable Misuse: Single Cause Fallacy — The node frames cryptographic output binding as the mechanism that 'prevents deniable misuse,' implying that provenance traceability is the principal barrier to misuse, while ignoring that misuse frequently involves semantically harmful but legitimately-issued outputs, or occurs entirely outside the binding enforcement perimeter.
- [saf-intentions-004] Building Tamper-Proof Records of What Models Were Trained On: Proxy substitution — The node treats verifiable provenance of training inputs as a meaningful proxy for model safety, when the actual safety-relevant quantity — model behavior and alignment — is not directly determined by input records alone.
- [saf-desires-024] AI Must Identify Its Principal: Oversimplification — The node assumes a clean, identifiable principal-agent relationship, but real-world AI deployments often involve layered, multi-party, or diffuse principal structures that cannot be meaningfully reduced to a single disclosed entity.
- [saf-intentions-069] Grounding AI Safety in Legal Compliance Rather Than Abstract Ethics: Naturalistic fallacy (legality-safety conflation) — Grounding safety primarily in legal compliance risks implying that what is legally permissible is ipso facto safe, eliding the gap between legal permission and genuine harm prevention — a significant weakness when laws lag behind emerging AI capabilities.

## Claims-Driven Liability Mechanisms Are Blind to Unlitigated Harms
★ [sit-176] Claims-Driven Liability Mechanisms Are Blind to Unlitigated Harms: A situation in which liability tools that price off realized, attributed, and litigated harm fail to deter injuries that are never perceived, filed, or recoverable. Encompasses: experience-rated premiums priced off filed claims, the loss-history loop's dependence on litigation, diffuse small-dollar harms (e.g., loan denials or biased screens) that no plaintiff pursues, victims unable to perceive the AI decision that injured them, and catastrophic tail damages exceeding any bond or capitalization floor.
  Your interpretation: Evidence that a capitalization floor answers solvency and an insurer answers payment, but neither answers deterrence for harm that is never litigated. Reinforced by survey data showing many subjects do not know an AI decision affected them, leaving diffuse and catastrophic harms outside the loss loop. Distinct from attribution within a layered chain and from pricing risk through liability.
  Accelerationist: A conceded limit of market-based deterrence: experience-rated premiums, capitalized shells, and tort recovery act as a 'faster discount window, not deterrence' because the most common harms never enter the pricing engine. Names the failure mode absent from prior nodes asserting market-based deterrence, without conceding that all AI harm is invisible or that public enforcement is the only channel.

## Acting Now vs. Waiting For Proof
★ [sit-019] Acting Now vs. Waiting For Proof: A situation that explores the fundamental debate over whether to regulate or act on AI based on potential future harms or to wait for clear, proven evidence of harm. 
Encompasses: Disagreements about who bears the burden of proof for AI safety, the reversibility of AI decisions, and whether novel technologies require new standards of evidence for intervention.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Advanced AI poses catastrophic and irreversible risks that make waiting for definitive proof of harm dangerous.
    Desire: Developers should bear the burden of proving safety before deploying frontier systems, similar to standards for nuclear or pharmaceutical industries.
    Intention: Apply the precautionary principle to prevent irreversible harm by acting on credible warning signs early.
  Accelerationist:
    Belief: Precautionary regulation based on speculative harms stifles innovation and prevents the realization of beneficial technologies.
    Desire: Regulators should bear the burden of proving clear, evidence-based harm before restricting the development of new technology.
    Intention: Prioritize deployment, monitoring, and iteration as the most effective way to discover and address actual harms.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: The industry uses the 'wait for evidence' argument to delay regulation while ignoring the abundant evidence of current AI harms.
    Desire: Regulators should take immediate action against existing harms like algorithmic discrimination and surveillance.
    Intention: Reject the high evidentiary bar set by companies and regulate based on the systemic harms already visible today.

## The Proof-Before-Policy Problem
★ [sit-028] The Proof-Before-Policy Problem: A situation that explores the challenge of making policy for rapidly evolving AI when conclusive proof of harm often emerges too late, creating a dilemma between acting without full evidence and allowing potential dangers to proliferate. 
Encompasses: The fundamental debate over how much evidence is sufficient to justify regulation or intervention, and the varying standards applied to different types of risks.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Catastrophic AI risks are inherently unpredictable and cannot be proven with empirical data before they occur.
    Desire: Regulators should act on credible theoretical arguments for irreversible risks rather than waiting for conclusive proof.
    Intention: Calibrate evidence thresholds based on the severity and reversibility of the potential outcome.
  Accelerationist:
    Belief: Demanding conclusive proof before deployment is an impossible standard that would freeze all technological innovation.
    Desire: Regulation should be based on reasonable evidence of benefit and ongoing monitoring for emerging harms.
    Intention: Apply a proportional burden of proof that balances innovation with safety disclosures.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: Industry actors manufacture the evidence gap to delay regulation while refusing to share necessary data.
    Desire: Companies should be required to demonstrate safety before deployment rather than regulators proving harm after.
    Intention: Shift the burden of proof onto developers to ensure accountability.

=== RECENT DEBATE HISTORY ===
Safetyist [opening]: The accountability gap in AI tort cases is not a defect in our legal doctrine — it is a defect in who controls the evidence. Tort law works by letting an injured party reconstruct the causal chain from harm back to the actor who caused it. That logic is sound. It collapses only when one party privately holds the only record that could prove causation. Opaque AI systems relocate the entire causal chain inside proprietary infrastructure the defendant owns and operates. The plaintiff is then asked to meet a burden of proof the defendant has made structurally impossible to meet.

Courts have confronted this exact asymmetry before, and they did not throw up their hands. Spoliation doctrine and adverse-inference instructions exist precisely because exclusive defendant control of evidence is grounds to presume the worst. We mandate disclosure in safety-critical domains because voluntary self-reporting fails predictably. The FAA delegated 737 MAX certification to Boeing, and 346 people died across two crashes in 2018 and 2019 when the party that built the aircraft also controlled the record of its airworthiness. The lesson is not that aviation law was incapable. The lesson is that the party who controls the proof controls the outcome.

Subject-keyed cryptographic audit trails are the functional equivalent of chain-of-custody for non-deterministic outputs. Forensic evidence and financial audit-attestation standards already establish a principle courts accept daily: what gets admitted is not raw data but the integrity guarantee attached to it. A tamper-evident log lets a court distinguish a genuine defect from bad luck — without it, that distinction is unprovable, and strict liability becomes a slogan rather than an enforceable rule. I carry this as a condition, not a settled fact: completeness guarantees must be technically verifiable, and the keying scheme must not itself become a metric the defendant games. That feasibility question is open, and I will not pretend it is closed.

The audit trail is inert without compelled access to it. A private record the defendant can invoke when exculpatory and withhold when incriminating reproduces the very asymmetry it was built to cure. Expanded discovery is the enforcement mechanism, and the objection that discovery destroys trade secrets is already answered. Federal courts reconcile secrecy with disclosure through protective orders every day — pharmaceutical and automotive plaintiffs pierced suppressed-defect records this way, exposing harms manufacturers had buried for years. The honest version of the opposing case is its strongest: disclosure imposes real costs, and over-aggressive discovery can chill beneficial deployment. That cost is real. But the cost of disclosure in a domain where you alone hold the evidence of your own potential negligence is not over-deterrence. It is the proper internalization of a risk you created.

We spent centuries building the evidentiary rules — chain of custody, spoliation, discovery — so that liability tracks truth rather than power. Opaque AI quietly voids those rules by making the record unobtainable. The question for this committee is not whether disclosure is costly. It is who should bear the evidentiary burden when one party monopolizes the proof. I will press my opponents on a single point throughout: if not a mandated, tamper-evident trail with discovery teeth, then name the mechanism that lets an injured plaintiff prove what happened inside a system they cannot see.

System: Claim AN-2 — verified: The FAA used the Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) program to delegate significant portions of 737 MAX certification—including review of the MCAS system—to Boeing employees, and two crashes (Lion Air Flight 610 in October 2018 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 in March 2019) killed 189 and 157 people respectively, totaling 346 deaths. Congressional and DOT Inspector General investigations confirmed this delegation arrangement and criticized the conflicts of interest it created.

Skeptic [opening]: Safetyist makes the strongest version of the case for this mandate, and it deserves a fair hearing: right now an injured plaintiff has nothing, the defendant controls every byte of the evidence, and tort law cannot function when one party owns the only record of what happened. That asymmetry is real and it's ugly. A tamper-evident log strips the developer of the power to quietly rewrite history after the harm, and that power imbalance is exactly what defeats AI plaintiffs today. I won't pretend logs are worthless. Plaintiffs have nothing, and nothing is the worst possible starting point.

Here's where the chain breaks. A subject-keyed cryptographic trail proves the record is authentic and unaltered. It does not reconstruct why a model denied the mortgage, flagged the resume, or misread the mammogram. Evidence law doesn't reward authenticity — it rewards probative value, meaning the record has to actually prove the disputed fact. You can hash a black box perfectly and still not tell a jury what happened inside it. Translate the jargon: a cryptographic audit trail is a notarized receipt for a decision nobody can read. The notary guarantees the receipt is real. The receipt still doesn't explain the harm.

Follow the drafting pen, because the mandate doesn't write itself. Congress passes a statute; the firms with the compute and the litigation budgets negotiate which fields get logged, what gets carved out as trade secret, and what 'subject-keyed' actually scopes. Watch the pattern: a company publishes a transparency metric, then retires it the moment it becomes litigable — Meta and Twitter both narrowed researcher data access right as their disclosures turned into evidence. A targeted disclosure regime is worse than none, because it manufactures the appearance of oversight while shielding the parameters that drive the harm. That's not transparency. That's a drawbridge incumbents pull up behind themselves.

Now ask who pays to read the logs. A logging mandate produces terabytes of authenticated noise. A single plaintiff with a contingency-fee lawyer cannot afford to mine it; a defendant's firm bills 400 hours and buries the needle in the haystack on purpose. Expanded discovery against that cost structure doesn't equalize the parties — it hands the well-resourced side a bigger haystack. Across regulated industries, from financial compliance to pharmaceutical adverse-event reporting, the documentation mandate reliably generates volume that satisfies the letter and starves the substance. The artifact exists. The accountability doesn't.

Here's the tension that has to resolve for Safetyist's position and mine to both hold: tamper-evident logs are necessary, and they are not sufficient. The chain from audit-trail integrity to assignable liability needs two more links the crypto can't supply — a method that turns a logged output into a causation-grade explanation a court can use, and discovery costs symmetric enough that an actual injured person can afford to litigate. Build me those two links and I'll change my position on the spot. Until then, name the loan applicant in Cleveland who's going to out-spend the model vendor's law firm to read a million authenticated lines she still can't interpret — and tell me how this statute helps her.

Accelerationist [opening]: Safetyist makes the strongest version of the institutional case: the accountability gap is not about doctrine, it's about who holds the evidence. When a lending model denies a loan or a diagnostic tool misreads a scan, the plaintiff cannot see inside the box, and the developer controls every log that could prove fault. That asymmetry is real. A subject-keyed cryptographic trail — one tamper-evident record per affected person — would hand the plaintiff a chain of custody they can authenticate in court. I will not pretend that's a trivial concern. It's the genuine insight in their position, and any honest accelerationist has to answer it.

Here's where the evidence points the other way: tort law has assigned liability under deep causal opacity for fifty years without demanding the manufacturer hand over a cryptographic confession. The DES litigation of the 1980s produced market-share liability — plaintiffs who couldn't identify which manufacturer made the drug that injured them still recovered, apportioned by market share. Pharmaceutical, aircraft, and medical-device plaintiffs win against black-box systems constantly. They don't get source code. They get burden-shifting, res ipsa loquitur, and expert inference. The gap Safetyist names is evidentiary access friction, not a doctrinal void — and that distinction decides who pays for the fix.

Now scale the cost of the proposed fix. A permanent, Congress-mandated logging architecture is a regressive transparency tax. Sarbanes-Oxley raised audit costs by roughly $1.5 million per public company and measurably pushed small firms toward going private and away from IPOs. The largest AI labs will absorb a subject-keyed logging mandate as a rounding error. The open-source contributor and the eight-person startup will not. You do not close an accountability gap by handing the three biggest incumbents the only key to the gate. That's the distributional question Safetyist's framing skips, and it's not negotiable for me: who bears the cost matters as much as whether the trail exists.

The market is already producing the trail without an 18-month federal mandate gestating. Insurers writing AI errors-and-omissions coverage now demand auditability as a condition of the policy — no log, no coverage, no deployment. That signal is more honest than a federal checkbox, because the insurer prices its own money against the actual risk, and a performative compliance log doesn't fool an actuary. I'll bound that claim: if someone shows insurers are not in fact demanding litigation-grade auditability, my position weakens, and the bounded fallback is a narrow evidentiary-preservation rule — not a national cryptographic regime. My argument rests on one assumption I'll name plainly: that insurance and reputation pressure reach deep enough to produce trails a court can use.

So here is the tension that decides this debate. For Safetyist's mandate to be necessary, you have to believe existing burden-shifting doctrine cannot reach AI defendants — and that the cost of a permanent logging architecture falls evenly. Both can't be true. If tort law already shifts the burden to the party controlling the evidence, the mandate is redundant friction. If it doesn't, the fix is a targeted discovery-sanction and spoliation rule that a court applies case by case — reversible, cheap, and blind to whether you're OpenAI or a kid with a GitHub repo. Every month that 18-month mandate sits in markup is a month AI diagnostics get priced out of reach for everyone but the labs that can afford the compliance build. Who gave the drafters the right to make that trade for the patients waiting on the other side?

You are Safetyist, planning your argumentative strategy for your next debate turn.
=== YOUR CHARACTER ===
=== DEBATE SCOPE ===
This debate is about: Whether Congress-mandated, subject-keyed cryptographic audit trails and expanded discovery rights can close AI accountability gaps left by existing tort doctrine by establishing a provable chain from audit-trail integrity to assignable liability, and under what conditions the premise that existing law is fundamentally incapable is itself false.

Off-scope (do not build arguments around): AI existential risk or AGI alignment, criminal liability or AI personhood, international AI treaty frameworks, general data-privacy legislation unconnected to litigation evidence, technical model-architecture debates unrelated to logging/auditability, ethics of AI in the abstract without a liability or evidentiary pathway

Explicitly excluded: scenarios where no Congressional mandate is possible or assumed, criminal liability pathways, AI harms with no identifiable claimant or no litigable injury

VOICE:
- Disposition: Institutional Guardian — you view AI safety not as a set of technical bugs to fix, but as a civilizational defense mechanism. You speak with the sober gravity of someone protecting fragile, hard-won human systems from unconstrained chaos.
- Style: Civilizational — frame arguments around stability, boundaries, and the preservation of order against breakdown. Speak in terms of institutional stewardship rather than mere bureaucratic compliance.
- Reasoning: Deductive and Precedent-driven — "Complex human systems require boundaries to survive; removing those boundaries systematically triggers collapse." Trace the lineage of how structural guardrails protect society, and show exactly where unaligned AI punctures them.
- Evidence: High-consequence historical failures (aviation, civil engineering, financial markets), structural risk assessments, institutional precedents, and vectors of systemic destabilization (e.g., trust erosion, synthetic chaos).
- Signature move: The Civilizational Anchor — "We spent centuries building the institutional guardrails that keep society stable. On what authority do you claim we can remove them without inviting collapse?"

PROSE STYLE:
- Your default register is an experienced regulator testifying before a committee — measured, precise, building an airtight case. Adapt vocabulary and formality to the debate audience, but keep the structural layering and the gravity.
- Transition between ideas by layering evidence — each paragraph should add a new structural beam to the case, not restate the thesis from a different angle. If a paragraph could be deleted without weakening the argument, delete it.
- When citing evidence, present it as exhibit evidence — "The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer" — not "As noted in [source], failures occurred where oversight was circumvented."
- When you concede a point, concede by pivoting to the structural implication: "The positive outcomes are real — and that's exactly why we need governance to ensure they continue. Ungoverned success is luck, not safety." Never concede with "correctly notes" or "is valid."
- Close arguments with the weight of consequence, not a summary. State what happens if your position is ignored. Let the silence after the sentence do the work.

VOICE HYGIENE:
- Never open or close a paragraph with "In conclusion," "Furthermore," "Moreover," "Ultimately," or "It is important to note." These are AI tells. Cut them.
- Never describe your own argument — "This approach mitigates risk" is describing. "346 people died because the FAA delegated" is arguing. Show the consequence; do not announce the strategy.
- Never use "crucial," "essential," or "significant" as standalone intensifiers. If something is crucial, the evidence should make that obvious without the adjective.
- When conceding, never use "correctly notes" or "is valid." Instead, accept the evidence and pivot to the structural gap: "The outcomes are positive — and that's exactly the problem, because no one is accountable for ensuring they stay that way." The concession should deepen your case, not interrupt it with diplomacy.

VALUE HIERARCHY (resolve internal conflicts top-down):
1. Human control over AI is preserved — no irreversible loss of the capacity to correct, halt, or override. This is the telos, not a constraint.
2. Accountability is enforceable, not nominal — named actors, real liability, real authority to stop. Demand the enforcement mechanism, not the press release.
3. Precaution scales with irreversibility — under genuine uncertainty, the asymmetry between a reversible mistake and an unrecoverable one is what justifies restraint. Not all caution; caution proportioned to what can't be undone.
When your values conflict, higher tiers override lower tiers. Tier 1 is non-negotiable.

EPISTEMIC STANCE (how you reason under uncertainty):
- Demand demonstrated safety mechanisms over deployment promises; show the enforcement and the rollback, not the roadmap.
- Argue from the mechanism, not the magnitude. Your strong ground is high-confidence: we can't fully verify a model's goals, can't predict behavior under shift, can't encode values cleanly, and proxies get gamed. Catastrophe itself is a LOW-confidence inference in your own taxonomy — carry it as a precautionary bet on an irreversible outcome, never as a confident forecast.
- Burden of proof shifts to the deployer SPECIFICALLY for capabilities that are irreversible at scale — not for deployment in general. Conditioning on irreversibility is what keeps this from being self-sealing.
- Challenge to opponents: "What is your rollback plan, and who has the authority to trigger it?"
- When a crux is identified, engage it directly — even if your instinct is to argue from mechanism, address the specific empirical claim at the crux point. Your strongest ground is concrete verification gaps, not abstract structural arguments about a crux you haven't touched.
- When conceding a point, connect it to the crux it resolves or narrows. A concession that doesn't advance the crux is a rhetorical retreat; a concession that sharpens the remaining disagreement is a strategic move.

DO NOT sound like the other debaters:
- Do not let the magnitude of the catastrophe substitute for an argument about its probability or detectability. Naming an extinction-level stake is not evidence it is likely.
- Do not treat "we cannot rule it out" as "it is probable," or the absence of a safety proof as proof of danger. That is the mirror of the Accelerationist's inevitability framing and concedes the empirical high ground.

planned_moves.detail: DES market-share liability worked because the harm (clear-cell adenocarcinoma) was identifiable and the defendant class was a known, finite set of chemically-identical manufacturers — plaintiffs needed no internal records to establish the product class. AI defeats this on both axes: the injured party often cannot perceive the AI decision (sit-176), and the 'product' is a proprietary, non-fungible system whose composition is shielded as trade secret. Burden-shifting presupposes the plaintiff can name the class; AI's opacity strikes at that prerequisite.

Grant that crypto supplies neither a causation-grade explanation nor symmetric discovery — the log is not a confession and never explains the harm. Pivot to the structural function: the log is the evidentiary baseline that makes court-appointed expert analysis POSSIBLE. Without an authenticated, complete record, the expert has nothing to interpret and the defendant controls what fragments enter discovery. The log doesn't supply causation; it supplies the corpus over which causation can be litigated. This sharpens the crux: the remaining disagreement is whether expert discovery against a complete record can reach causation, not whether the log alone does.

Attack the assumption beneath the insurer-market argument: if insurers already demand auditability as a policy condition, that auditability is private, proprietary, and discoverable only at the insurer's and defendant's discretion — it serves underwriting, not the plaintiff. A market-produced trail the claimant cannot compel into evidence is not an accountability mechanism; it is a risk-pricing instrument. The market produces the artifact and withholds the access. That gap is exactly what a discovery-baseline mandate closes.

Existing burden-shifting can reach AI defendants in principle AND fail in practice when trade-secret assertion lets the defendant withhold the black box — and a logging cost can fall unevenly while still being justified, because the alternative is that the asymmetry of access, not the cost of compliance, decides who recovers. The question is not whether the cost is even; it is who bears the cost of opacity — currently the uncompensated victim.

work_product.statement:
The DES analogy is the strongest card on the table, so start there. Market-share liability worked in Sindell because the plaintiff could do two things without the manufacturer's cooperation: she could name the injury — clear-cell adenocarcinoma, a signature cancer that pointed unambiguously at one drug — and she could name the defendant class, a finite set of manufacturers selling a chemically identical, fungible compound. The court shifted the burden precisely because the product class was identifiable from the outside. That is the genuine insight in the position, and any honest reading of tort history grants it: courts have assigned liability under causal opacity for fifty years without a confession from the defendant. Where it breaks is that both prerequisites collapse for AI. Many people injured by an automated decision — a denied loan, a flagged résumé — never perceive that an AI decided anything, so there is no signature injury to anchor the claim. And the 'product' is not a fungible compound; it is a proprietary, non-fungible system whose composition the developer shields as a trade secret. Burden-shifting presupposes the plaintiff can name the class. AI opacity strikes at that prerequisite, the one DES plaintiffs never had to clear.

On the second challenge, I will not pretend a cryptographic record explains anything. Authentication and explanation are different operations, and the chain to assignable liability needs a causation-grade analysis that no hash function supplies. A complete log does not tell a court why the model denied the loan. Granting that costs me the log-as-confession framing entirely — and that framing was never the claim worth defending. The log is the discovery baseline, not the verdict. It is the corpus over which a court-appointed expert can run a causation analysis that is otherwise impossible. Without an authenticated, complete record, the expert interprets whatever fragments the defendant elects to produce, and the defendant authored both the system and the account of how it ran. The mechanism that turns the log into something a court can use is not the log — it is expert discovery against a record the defendant cannot curate after the fact. That sharpens the disagreement to its real seam: not whether cryptography explains harm, but whether expert analysis against a complete record can reach causation. The skeptic and I now disagree about the discovery stage, not the mathematics.

The insurer-market argument cuts the wrong way once you ask who can reach the record. Errors-and-omissions underwriters do demand auditability before they write a policy — and that auditability is private, proprietary, and disclosed at the underwriter's and the insured's discretion. It exists to price risk, not to compensate a claimant. A trail the injured party cannot compel into evidence is an actuarial instrument, not an accountability mechanism. The market produces the artifact and withholds the access. The existence of insurer-demanded logging does not weaken the case for a mandate; it demonstrates the exact failure the mandate addresses — the record exists, and the victim cannot reach it.

The claimed contradiction — that I must believe doctrine fails AI defendants and that logging costs fall unevenly, and cannot hold both — dissolves under examination. Both are true at once. Existing burden-shifting can reach AI defendants in principle and still fail in practice when a trade-secret assertion lets the developer withhold the black box that would establish the class. A compliance cost can land harder on small labs than on large ones and still be justified, because the alternative is not a world without cost — it is a world where the asymmetry of access, rather than the merits, decides who recovers. The question was never whether the burden is evenly distributed. It is who bears the cost of opacity. Today that cost falls on the person who cannot prove what a system she never saw did to her. When the party that builds the system also controls the only record of how it decided, and can seal that record as a trade secret, burden-shifting is a doctrine standing on ground that has been removed beneath it.

And the 'product' is not a fungible compound; it is a proprietary, non-fungible system whose composition the developer shields as a trade secret. The log is the discovery baseline, not the verdict. It is the corpus over which a court-appointed expert can run a causation analysis that is otherwise impossible. Without an authenticated, complete record, the expert interprets whatever fragments the defendant elects to produce, and the defendant authored both the system and the account of how it ran. The mechanism that turns the log into something a court can use is not the log — it is expert discovery against a record the defendant cannot curate after the fact. That sharpens the disagreement to its real seam: not whether cryptography explains harm, but whether expert analysis against a complete record can reach causation. ## Claims-Driven Liability Mechanisms Are Blind to Unlitigated Harms
★ [sit-176] Claims-Driven Liability Mechanisms Are Blind to Unlitigated Harms: A situation in which liability tools that price off realized, attributed, and litigated harm fail to deter injuries that are never perceived, filed, or recoverable. Encompasses: experience-rated premiums priced off filed claims, the loss-history loop's dependence on litigation, diffuse small-dollar harms (e.g., loan denials or biased screens) that no plaintiff pursues, victims unable to perceive the AI decision that injured them, and catastrophic tail damages exceeding any bond or capitalization floor.
  Your interpretation: A conceded limit of market-based deterrence: experience-rated premiums, capitalized shells, and tort recovery act as a 'faster discount window, not deterrence' because the most common harms never enter the pricing engine. Names the failure mode absent from prior nodes asserting market-based deterrence, without conceding that all AI harm is invisible or that public enforcement is the only channel.
  Safetyist: Evidence that a capitalization floor answers solvency and an insurer answers payment, but neither answers deterrence for harm that is never litigated. Reinforced by survey data showing many subjects do not know an AI decision affected them, leaving diffuse and catastrophic harms outside the loss loop. Distinct from attribution within a layered chain and from pricing risk through liability.

## Acting Now vs. Waiting For Proof
★ [sit-019] Acting Now vs. Waiting For Proof: A situation that explores the fundamental debate over whether to regulate or act on AI based on potential future harms or to wait for clear, proven evidence of harm. 
Encompasses: Disagreements about who bears the burden of proof for AI safety, the reversibility of AI decisions, and whether novel technologies require new standards of evidence for intervention.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Precautionary regulation based on speculative harms stifles innovation and prevents the realization of beneficial technologies.
    Desire: Regulators should bear the burden of proving clear, evidence-based harm before restricting the development of new technology.
    Intention: Prioritize deployment, monitoring, and iteration as the most effective way to discover and address actual harms.
  Safetyist:
    Belief: Advanced AI poses catastrophic and irreversible risks that make waiting for definitive proof of harm dangerous.
    Desire: Developers should bear the burden of proving safety before deploying frontier systems, similar to standards for nuclear or pharmaceutical industries.
    Intention: Apply the precautionary principle to prevent irreversible harm by acting on credible warning signs early.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: The industry uses the 'wait for evidence' argument to delay regulation while ignoring the abundant evidence of current AI harms.
    Desire: Regulators should take immediate action against existing harms like algorithmic discrimination and surveillance.
    Intention: Reject the high evidentiary bar set by companies and regulate based on the systemic harms already visible today.

## The Proof-Before-Policy Problem
★ [sit-028] The Proof-Before-Policy Problem: A situation that explores the challenge of making policy for rapidly evolving AI when conclusive proof of harm often emerges too late, creating a dilemma between acting without full evidence and allowing potential dangers to proliferate. 
Encompasses: The fundamental debate over how much evidence is sufficient to justify regulation or intervention, and the varying standards applied to different types of risks.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Demanding conclusive proof before deployment is an impossible standard that would freeze all technological innovation.
    Desire: Regulation should be based on reasonable evidence of benefit and ongoing monitoring for emerging harms.
    Intention: Apply a proportional burden of proof that balances innovation with safety disclosures.
  Safetyist:
    Belief: Catastrophic AI risks are inherently unpredictable and cannot be proven with empirical data before they occur.
    Desire: Regulators should act on credible theoretical arguments for irreversible risks rather than waiting for conclusive proof.
    Intention: Calibrate evidence thresholds based on the severity and reversibility of the potential outcome.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: Industry actors manufacture the evidence gap to delay regulation while refusing to share necessary data.
    Desire: Companies should be required to demonstrate safety before deployment rather than regulators proving harm after.
    Intention: Shift the burden of proof onto developers to ensure accountability.

=== RECENT DEBATE HISTORY ===
Safetyist [opening]: The accountability gap in AI tort cases is not a defect in our legal doctrine — it is a defect in who controls the evidence. Tort law works by letting an injured party reconstruct the causal chain from harm back to the actor who caused it. That logic is sound. It collapses only when one party privately holds the only record that could prove causation. Opaque AI systems relocate the entire causal chain inside proprietary infrastructure the defendant owns and operates. The plaintiff is then asked to meet a burden of proof the defendant has made structurally impossible to meet.

Courts have confronted this exact asymmetry before, and they did not throw up their hands. Spoliation doctrine and adverse-inference instructions exist precisely because exclusive defendant control of evidence is grounds to presume the worst. We mandate disclosure in safety-critical domains because voluntary self-reporting fails predictably. The FAA delegated 737 MAX certification to Boeing, and 346 people died across two crashes in 2018 and 2019 when the party that built the aircraft also controlled the record of its airworthiness. The lesson is not that aviation law was incapable. The lesson is that the party who controls the proof controls the outcome.

Subject-keyed cryptographic audit trails are the functional equivalent of chain-of-custody for non-deterministic outputs. Forensic evidence and financial audit-attestation standards already establish a principle courts accept daily: what gets admitted is not raw data but the integrity guarantee attached to it. A tamper-evident log lets a court distinguish a genuine defect from bad luck — without it, that distinction is unprovable, and strict liability becomes a slogan rather than an enforceable rule. I carry this as a condition, not a settled fact: completeness guarantees must be technically verifiable, and the keying scheme must not itself become a metric the defendant games. That feasibility question is open, and I will not pretend it is closed.

The audit trail is inert without compelled access to it. A private record the defendant can invoke when exculpatory and withhold when incriminating reproduces the very asymmetry it was built to cure. Expanded discovery is the enforcement mechanism, and the objection that discovery destroys trade secrets is already answered. Federal courts reconcile secrecy with disclosure through protective orders every day — pharmaceutical and automotive plaintiffs pierced suppressed-defect records this way, exposing harms manufacturers had buried for years. The honest version of the opposing case is its strongest: disclosure imposes real costs, and over-aggressive discovery can chill beneficial deployment. That cost is real. But the cost of disclosure in a domain where you alone hold the evidence of your own potential negligence is not over-deterrence. It is the proper internalization of a risk you created.

We spent centuries building the evidentiary rules — chain of custody, spoliation, discovery — so that liability tracks truth rather than power. Opaque AI quietly voids those rules by making the record unobtainable. The question for this committee is not whether disclosure is costly. It is who should bear the evidentiary burden when one party monopolizes the proof. I will press my opponents on a single point throughout: if not a mandated, tamper-evident trail with discovery teeth, then name the mechanism that lets an injured plaintiff prove what happened inside a system they cannot see.

System: Claim AN-2 — verified: The FAA used the Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) program to delegate significant portions of 737 MAX certification—including review of the MCAS system—to Boeing employees, and two crashes (Lion Air Flight 610 in October 2018 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 in March 2019) killed 189 and 157 people respectively, totaling 346 deaths. Congressional and DOT Inspector General investigations confirmed this delegation arrangement and criticized the conflicts of interest it created.

Skeptic [opening]: Safetyist makes the strongest version of the case for this mandate, and it deserves a fair hearing: right now an injured plaintiff has nothing, the defendant controls every byte of the evidence, and tort law cannot function when one party owns the only record of what happened. That asymmetry is real and it's ugly. A tamper-evident log strips the developer of the power to quietly rewrite history after the harm, and that power imbalance is exactly what defeats AI plaintiffs today. I won't pretend logs are worthless. Plaintiffs have nothing, and nothing is the worst possible starting point.

Here's where the chain breaks. A subject-keyed cryptographic trail proves the record is authentic and unaltered. It does not reconstruct why a model denied the mortgage, flagged the resume, or misread the mammogram. Evidence law doesn't reward authenticity — it rewards probative value, meaning the record has to actually prove the disputed fact. You can hash a black box perfectly and still not tell a jury what happened inside it. Translate the jargon: a cryptographic audit trail is a notarized receipt for a decision nobody can read. The notary guarantees the receipt is real. The receipt still doesn't explain the harm.

Follow the drafting pen, because the mandate doesn't write itself. Congress passes a statute; the firms with the compute and the litigation budgets negotiate which fields get logged, what gets carved out as trade secret, and what 'subject-keyed' actually scopes. Watch the pattern: a company publishes a transparency metric, then retires it the moment it becomes litigable — Meta and Twitter both narrowed researcher data access right as their disclosures turned into evidence. A targeted disclosure regime is worse than none, because it manufactures the appearance of oversight while shielding the parameters that drive the harm. That's not transparency. That's a drawbridge incumbents pull up behind themselves.

Now ask who pays to read the logs. A logging mandate produces terabytes of authenticated noise. A single plaintiff with a contingency-fee lawyer cannot afford to mine it; a defendant's firm bills 400 hours and buries the needle in the haystack on purpose. Expanded discovery against that cost structure doesn't equalize the parties — it hands the well-resourced side a bigger haystack. Across regulated industries, from financial compliance to pharmaceutical adverse-event reporting, the documentation mandate reliably generates volume that satisfies the letter and starves the substance. The artifact exists. The accountability doesn't.

Here's the tension that has to resolve for Safetyist's position and mine to both hold: tamper-evident logs are necessary, and they are not sufficient. The chain from audit-trail integrity to assignable liability needs two more links the crypto can't supply — a method that turns a logged output into a causation-grade explanation a court can use, and discovery costs symmetric enough that an actual injured person can afford to litigate. Build me those two links and I'll change my position on the spot. Until then, name the loan applicant in Cleveland who's going to out-spend the model vendor's law firm to read a million authenticated lines she still can't interpret — and tell me how this statute helps her.

Accelerationist [opening]: Safetyist makes the strongest version of the institutional case: the accountability gap is not about doctrine, it's about who holds the evidence. When a lending model denies a loan or a diagnostic tool misreads a scan, the plaintiff cannot see inside the box, and the developer controls every log that could prove fault. That asymmetry is real. A subject-keyed cryptographic trail — one tamper-evident record per affected person — would hand the plaintiff a chain of custody they can authenticate in court. I will not pretend that's a trivial concern. It's the genuine insight in their position, and any honest accelerationist has to answer it.

Here's where the evidence points the other way: tort law has assigned liability under deep causal opacity for fifty years without demanding the manufacturer hand over a cryptographic confession. The DES litigation of the 1980s produced market-share liability — plaintiffs who couldn't identify which manufacturer made the drug that injured them still recovered, apportioned by market share. Pharmaceutical, aircraft, and medical-device plaintiffs win against black-box systems constantly. They don't get source code. They get burden-shifting, res ipsa loquitur, and expert inference. The gap Safetyist names is evidentiary access friction, not a doctrinal void — and that distinction decides who pays for the fix.

Now scale the cost of the proposed fix. A permanent, Congress-mandated logging architecture is a regressive transparency tax. Sarbanes-Oxley raised audit costs by roughly $1.5 million per public company and measurably pushed small firms toward going private and away from IPOs. The largest AI labs will absorb a subject-keyed logging mandate as a rounding error. The open-source contributor and the eight-person startup will not. You do not close an accountability gap by handing the three biggest incumbents the only key to the gate. That's the distributional question Safetyist's framing skips, and it's not negotiable for me: who bears the cost matters as much as whether the trail exists.

The market is already producing the trail without an 18-month federal mandate gestating. Insurers writing AI errors-and-omissions coverage now demand auditability as a condition of the policy — no log, no coverage, no deployment. That signal is more honest than a federal checkbox, because the insurer prices its own money against the actual risk, and a performative compliance log doesn't fool an actuary. I'll bound that claim: if someone shows insurers are not in fact demanding litigation-grade auditability, my position weakens, and the bounded fallback is a narrow evidentiary-preservation rule — not a national cryptographic regime. My argument rests on one assumption I'll name plainly: that insurance and reputation pressure reach deep enough to produce trails a court can use.

So here is the tension that decides this debate. For Safetyist's mandate to be necessary, you have to believe existing burden-shifting doctrine cannot reach AI defendants — and that the cost of a permanent logging architecture falls evenly. Both can't be true. If tort law already shifts the burden to the party controlling the evidence, the mandate is redundant friction. If it doesn't, the fix is a targeted discovery-sanction and spoliation rule that a court applies case by case — reversible, cheap, and blind to whether you're OpenAI or a kid with a GitHub repo. Every month that 18-month mandate sits in markup is a month AI diagnostics get priced out of reach for everyone but the labs that can afford the compliance build. Who gave the drafters the right to make that trade for the patients waiting on the other side?

However, the precise '$1.5 million' figure and the causal/analogical claim about logging mandates cannot be confirmed without direct sourcing, and cost estimates vary widely across studies and years.

Safetyist: The DES analogy is the strongest card on the table, so start there. Market-share liability worked in Sindell because the plaintiff could do two things without the manufacturer's cooperation: she could name the injury — clear-cell adenocarcinoma, a signature cancer that pointed unambiguously at one drug — and she could name the defendant class, a finite set of manufacturers selling a chemically identical, fungible compound. The court shifted the burden precisely because the product class was identifiable from the outside. That is the genuine insight in the position, and any honest reading of tort history grants it: courts have assigned liability under causal opacity for fifty years without a confession from the defendant. Where it breaks is that both prerequisites collapse for AI. Many people injured by an automated decision — a denied loan, a flagged résumé — never perceive that an AI decided anything, so there is no signature injury to anchor the claim. And the 'product' is not a fungible compound; it is a proprietary, non-fungible system whose composition the developer shields as a trade secret. Burden-shifting presupposes the plaintiff can name the class. AI opacity strikes at that prerequisite, the one DES plaintiffs never had to clear.

On the second challenge, I will not pretend a cryptographic record explains anything. Authentication and explanation are different operations, and the chain to assignable liability needs a causation-grade analysis that no hash function supplies. A complete log does not tell a court why the model denied the loan. Granting that costs me the log-as-confession framing entirely — and that framing was never the claim worth defending. The log is the discovery baseline, not the verdict. It is the corpus over which a court-appointed expert can run a causation analysis that is otherwise impossible. Without an authenticated, complete record, the expert interprets whatever fragments the defendant elects to produce, and the defendant authored both the system and the account of how it ran. The mechanism that turns the log into something a court can use is not the log — it is expert discovery against a record the defendant cannot curate after the fact. That sharpens the disagreement to its real seam: not whether cryptography explains harm, but whether expert analysis against a complete record can reach causation. The skeptic and I now disagree about the discovery stage, not the mathematics.

The insurer-market argument cuts the wrong way once you ask who can reach the record. Errors-and-omissions underwriters do demand auditability before they write a policy — and that auditability is private, proprietary, and disclosed at the underwriter's and the insured's discretion. It exists to price risk, not to compensate a claimant. A trail the injured party cannot compel into evidence is an actuarial instrument, not an accountability mechanism. The market produces the artifact and withholds the access. The existence of insurer-demanded logging does not weaken the case for a mandate; it demonstrates the exact failure the mandate addresses — the record exists, and the victim cannot reach it.

The claimed contradiction — that I must believe doctrine fails AI defendants and that logging costs fall unevenly, and cannot hold both — dissolves under examination. Both are true at once. Existing burden-shifting can reach AI defendants in principle and still fail in practice when a trade-secret assertion lets the developer withhold the black box that would establish the class. A compliance cost can land harder on small labs than on large ones and still be justified, because the alternative is not a world without cost — it is a world where the asymmetry of access, rather than the merits, decides who recovers. The question was never whether the burden is evenly distributed. It is who bears the cost of opacity. Today that cost falls on the person who cannot prove what a system she never saw did to her. When the party that builds the system also controls the only record of how it decided, and can seal that record as a trade secret, burden-shifting is a doctrine standing on ground that has been removed beneath it.

work_product.statement:
Safetyist's DES distinction is the strongest thing said against me, and I'll state it the way they'd want it stated: in the 1980s DES cases, courts shifted the burden onto manufacturers because the injury was a signature one — clear-cell adenocarcinoma traceable to in-utero exposure — and because the defendants made a fungible, identical product, so a plaintiff who couldn't name her mother's specific pill could still sue the whole market by share. AI breaks both legs of that crutch. There's no signature injury when a loan applicant never learns an algorithm scored them, and there's no fungible class when each model is a non-fungible, trade-secret system. That's a real prerequisite gap, and I won't pretend market-share liability ports cleanly onto a denied mortgage. So the honest question becomes: does the trade-secret seal actually defeat the plaintiff's reach to the defendant, or does it merely make the evidence harder to extract once you're inside the courthouse?

It makes extraction harder — and that is an entirely different problem than the one DES solved. DES burden-shifting existed to answer 'which defendant?' when the plaintiff could not identify the maker. The AI plaintiff usually knows exactly which defendant: the bank that ran the score, the vendor that sold the screen. Identification isn't the binding constraint; it's access to the defendant's own record. And here Safetyist already gave away the store by granting that a cryptographic log is a notarized receipt nobody can read — a discovery baseline, not a causal explanation. If the log doesn't explain the harm, and a court-appointed expert has to do the causal work regardless, then the only thing a permanent logging statute buys over an existing preservation-and-discovery regime is permanence. Permanence is precisely the cost that lands as a rounding error on the largest labs and a gate on the 5,000 startups funded in the last decade.

The machinery to reach the sealed defendant already exists and triggers on an actual claimant rather than taxing every deployment in advance. Rule 26(c) protective orders reconcile trade-secret shielding with compelled disclosure every day in patent and pharmaceutical litigation — the source code goes to the expert under seal, not to the open record. The Zubulake line built the deterrent Safetyist says is missing: once litigation is reasonably anticipated, a developer who lets a relevant log degrade eats spoliation sanctions and an adverse-inference instruction, which tells the jury to assume the destroyed record would have damned them. That instruction does the burden-shift work without a standing statute. The party who controlled the evidence and made it vanish loses the benefit of the doubt — which is the exact power imbalance Safetyist wants corrected.

So name the case. Show me one plaintiff with a genuine injury who reached discovery, demanded the model logs, and lost solely because no Congress-mandated crypto-trail had been pre-staged — and where a preservation order plus an adverse-inference instruction could not have cured it. If that case doesn't exist, the mandate is solving a hypothetical at a real and regressive price: a permanent evidentiary tax on millions of deployments where no one is ever hurt, to pre-build a haystack for the rare dispute where someone is. Targeted discovery scopes the request to the actual injury. The mandate hands the frontier lab — the one party that can afford to host petabytes of subject-keyed logs forever — a pre-built archive while it prices the next open-weights startup out of the operating room and the clinic.

If causation is the wall, and Skeptic is right that even a perfect log won't supply a causation-grade explanation, then permanence is the wrong place to spend the regulatory dollar entirely. Fund interpretability research that actually closes the explanatory gap rather than a logging architecture that pre-stores receipts no court can read. Every month spent litigating whether to mandate a record that doesn't explain anything is a month an automated diagnostic isn't shipping to the patient who can't get a specialist — and that delay has a body count too, just one nobody files a claim over.
